title: perf incident postmortem - SLO miss and hotfix validation (2026-03)
body:
Summary:

On 2026-03-03 we observed a regression causing p95 request latency to increase above the SLO for the hosted inference tier. The incident lasted ~2h from first alert to stabilization; ~15% of traffic to the affected model family experienced p95 latency spikes (baseline p95 ~120ms, spike p95 ~420-480ms). Customer-facing error rates did not increase significantly, but latency SLOs were violated and a priority customer opened an escalation.

Impact:
- SLO: p95 latency > 300ms for hosted-api model-family (hosted:general-purpose)
- Duration: ~02:10 UTC -> ~04:30 UTC on 2026-03-03
- Affected traffic: ~15% of requests routed to weight-optimized pool in us-west
- Customers: 1 priority customer escalated to CS; several internal alerts (on-call and infra) triggered

Timeline (UTC):
- 02:10 - SLO alert triggered (p95 breach) from observability rule "serving.p95.slo.hosted"
- 02:12 - On-call (Marcus) acknowledged, opened PD incident PD-46532
- 02:20 - Initial triage: high GPU utilization + increase in queueing latency observed on serving nodes in weight-optimized pool
- 02:35 - Profiling snapshots started (perfetto + NVTX + custom tracing) across 5 representative pods
- 02:55 - Identified increased CPU->GPU memcpy durations and elevated kernel runtime on attention layers for long sequences
- 03:20 - Rollback candidate prepared: revert batching heuristic change from release 2026-03-02 (PR #987)
- 03:32 - Hotfix deployed to canary (5% traffic), observed p95 return close to baseline in canary
- 03:55 - Hotfix promoted to remaining nodes via controlled rollout; by 04:30 p95 stabilized within SLO

Root cause (summary):
A recent change shipped on 2026-03-02 modified the dynamic batching heuristic and kernel selection fallback logic intended to favor lower-latency kernels for short sequences. Under the observed production workload (a higher-than-normal fraction of medium-length prompts ~1k tokens and more prefix reuse), the heuristic caused requests to be batched into larger groups and select a fallback quantized kernel for certain layers. This combination increased per-request queueing time and introduced slower kernel runtimes for affected layers, compounded by increased CPU->GPU memcpy stall time due to slightly larger batch sizes. In short: heuristic + kernel-fallback path + workload distribution => increased p95 latency.

Investigation details & profiling findings:
- Sampling: collected NVTX traces, kernel timelines, and flamegraphs from affected pods (5 pods across two hosts).
- CPU/GPU metrics: host CPU idle decreased moderately, GPU utilization increased by ~8-10% on affected hosts, but NVLINK and PCIe write stalls increased during spikes.
- Memcpy traces: observed 1.6x increase in average memcpy time (CPU->GPU) during spike windows. This correlated with larger effective batch sizes in the batching queue.
- Kernel runtimes: attention kernel fallback (quantized path) had higher variance and a ~1.8x median runtime for some mid-length sequences due to suboptimal tiling chosen by fallback path.
- Queueing: continuous batching queue length increased ~2.5x for a subset of requests; queueing latency accounted for ~45% of the p95 increase.
- Cache behavior: KV-cache eviction rate increased for some pods resulting in additional recompute for prefixes; this was secondary but contributed to tail.

Hypothesis validated by A/B tests:
- Reverting the batching heuristic on a canary returned p95 to baseline under replicated traffic patterns (locally and in canary).
- Forcing the primary kernel selection (avoid fallback) also reduced p95, but revealed a small throughput regression for extremely short sequences. Tradeoff required the revert approach for immediate mitigation.

Hotfix & validation details:
- Hotfix: revert the batching heuristic change and adjust kernel fallback ordering to prefer primary kernels when batch size < 8 and sequence length between 256-2048 tokens. Small patch also increased KV-cache high-water threshold to reduce eviction churn. (PR linked: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/987)
- Canary validation: deployed to 5% traffic (two nodes) and ran 30 minutes of live traffic shadowing plus synthetic load with real prompt distribution (from ingress sampling). Metrics observed: p95 dropped from ~460ms -> ~130ms; q95 and cpu/gpu metrics returned to baseline.
- Gradual rollout: 5% -> 25% -> 60% -> 100 over ~1h with automated monitors and manual checkpoints. No regression observed during rollout.
- Post-deploy validation: continued 6h elevated monitoring window; no further SLO breaches in the affected pool.

Mitigations and long-term fixes (proposed):
- Short term (1 week): ship the hotfix revert + fallback ordering change (done). Update runbooks to include quick rollback steps for batching heuristic changes. Add an automated canary test that replays ingress distribution for 30 minutes after deploy.
- Medium term (4 weeks): improve kernel selection telemetry (per-layer selection stats surfaced in dashboards), add unit/integration tests that simulate mixed prompt-length distributions and verify p95 under synthetic load. Tune continuous batching parameters dynamically based on observed sequence-length histogram.
- Long term (quarter): invest in adaptive kernel-selection ML model that predicts best kernel per request shape, and a scheduler that limits batch coalescing when median latency risks rising.

Action items (owners):
- Aisha: finalize postmortem doc + update Confluence (due 2026-03-06)
- Marcus: instrument per-layer kernel selection counts + add dashboard panels (due 2026-03-10)
- Lena: add canary replay test to CI that uses sampled ingress distribution (due 2026-03-12)
- Omar: add integration test for KV-cache high-water behavior under mixed-length sequences (due 2026-03-17)
- Priya: update runbook and rollback playbook for batching heuristic changes (due 2026-03-05)

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Why did the batching heuristic favor larger groups for medium-length prompts even when the CPU->GPU memcpy cost was expected to dominate? Need deeper simulation of batching decision boundary.
- Is there a workload shift (customer-side) that changed sequence length distributions? Ask CS to surface any recent product changes that could explain the distribution shift.
- Consider automating safe kernel fallback testing in CI to avoid regressions when adding new kernel paths.

Notes & rough scratch items (raw):
- Observability gap: we didn't have a direct metric for per-request kernel variant chosen; added that now but need historical backfill.
- Quick win: limit max batching window to 12ms for weight-optimized pool as a safety cap (followup PR).
- Customer comms draft in Confluence (linked).

Appendix (commands & checks used during triage):
- nvprof / nsys traces collected to s3: s3://perf-collection/2026-03-03/PD-46532/
- sample command: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- /bin/sh -c 'cat /proc/interrupts; nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory --format=csv'
notes: Informal notes: parts of this doc are rough; need to clean before posting to exec channel. Some TODOs are owner-assigned above. We should schedule a 30m postmortem sync with CS for customer-facing messaging.
